743.title: Ja'far's speech
743.hook: Ja'far explains to the Negus: we lived in ignorance and cruelty, then a man came teaching truth, kinship and mercy (sirah)
743.howItsDone: Muslims retell Ja'far's speech to the Negus in sirah lessons and sermons as a summary of what the Prophet's message changed in his community's way of living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the emigrants crossed the sea. Your line was: a just king. Did you thank a fair person, or use a little power so no one was wronged? Day seven hundred forty-three.

Two envoys from Quraysh arrive at the Negus's court with gifts of leather, and something for each of the king's patricians first. Their request: these runaways have abandoned our religion and haven't taken yours. Hand them back. The patricians agree. But the king won't hand anyone over without hearing them. So the Muslims are summoned, and they have to decide, quickly, what they're going to say. Umm Salamah, who was there, says they agreed on this: we will say what we know, and what our Prophet told us, whatever comes of it. Today: Ja'far's speech.
screen: `GIFTS FOR THE KING.` → `HAND THEM BACK.` → `SAY WHAT WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: The one who speaks for them is Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin. Umm Salamah's report, kept in Musnad Ahmad, gives the speech, and here it is in paraphrase. O king, we were a people living in ignorance. We worshipped idols, ate dead animals, did shameful things, cut our ties of family, treated our neighbors badly, and the strong among us devoured the weak. Then God sent us a messenger from among us, whose family, truthfulness, trustworthiness and purity we knew. He called us to worship God alone and leave the stones our fathers had served. He told us to speak the truth, to keep our trusts, to hold to our kin, to be good to our neighbors, and to stop the bloodshed. Then our own people turned on us, so we came to your land, choosing you, hoping not to be wronged near you. Listen to how it's built. He doesn't start with doctrine. He starts with a confession: this is what we were. Then the change, and the change is mostly about how people treat each other: truth, trust, family, neighbors, the weak. Today's line names three threads of it: truth, kinship, mercy. Notice also what he leaves out. He doesn't insult the envoys, or their gods, or the king's faith. He tells a before and after, and lets the king judge. And the king is listening.
screen: `THIS IS WHAT WE WERE.` · `A MAN WHOSE TRUTHFULNESS WE KNEW.` · `TRUTH, TRUST, KIN, NEIGHBORS.` · `NO INSULTS. A BEFORE AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: The practice: explain your values in three sentences. Settle and breathe. Then, without hurrying, find them. One sentence for where you came from, or what you used to be like. One for what changed you, or who. One for what you now try to do, plainly, about how you treat people. No big words, no argument with anyone. Just the three sentences, the way you'd say them to a stranger who had the power to send you away. Say them once in your head, then once softly aloud. The bell holds the time.
Ja'far's speech. Before the Negus, Ja'far tells what his people were, who came to them, and what he taught: truth, trust, kinship, neighbors, an end to bloodshed. Today's word.
Your line: truth, kinship, mercy. Today, if someone asks what you stand for, answer with how you treat people before you answer with anything else. Day seven hundred forty-three.

what a scholar hears: Umm Salamah's report in Musnad Ahmad, the envoys' gifts to the patricians first, and the list: truth, trust, kinship, neighbors.

744.title: The Negus weeps
744.hook: Ja'far recites Surah Maryam, and the Christian king weeps and refuses to hand them over (sirah)
744.howItsDone: Muslims honor the Negus, al-Najashi, in sirah lessons as the Christian king who sheltered the emigrants, and Ja'far's recitation of surah Maryam before him is retold as a story of shared reverence for Mary and Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ja'far's speech before the king. Your line was: truth, kinship, mercy. Did you find your three sentences, and did anyone hear them? Day seven hundred forty-four.

Ja'far has finished. The court is quiet. The envoys from Mecca are waiting for the king to send the runaways home. His bishops have their books open around him. And the Negus asks one question. Not about politics, not about the gifts. He asks: do you have with you anything of what your prophet brought from God? Ja'far says yes. Read it to me, says the king. Ja'far has to choose, on the spot, which words to read to a Christian king in a Christian court. Today: the Negus weeps.
screen: `THE COURT IS QUIET.` → `DO YOU HAVE ANY OF IT WITH YOU?` → `READ IT TO ME.`

segments.voice: Umm Salamah says Ja'far recited the opening of surah Maryam, the surah named for Mary. It tells of Zachariah praying in secret for a child in his old age, of John, and then of Mary herself. In Pickthall's words, a verse of it begins: "And make mention of Mary in the Scripture." It goes on to the angel who comes to her, and the birth of her son, Jesus. Look at the choice. Ja'far didn't read the passages a king might find hardest. He read the ones about the figures this court's own faith honored, as the Qur'an tells them. And Umm Salamah says the Negus wept until his beard was wet, and his bishops wept until the pages in front of them were wet. Then the king spoke. In her telling, he said that this and what Moses brought came from the same lamp; in Ibn Ishaq's version of the scene, it is what Jesus brought. And he turned to the envoys: go. I will not hand them over to you. Later he gave back the gifts Quraysh had sent. Umm Salamah has him say that he would not take a mountain of gold to harm a single one of them. Notice who the hero of this chapter is. Not a companion. A Christian king, who listened, was moved, and protected strangers who had nothing to give him. Muslims tell his story with honor. The tears came first. The protection followed.
screen: `HE READ THE SURAH OF MARY.` · `THE KING WEPT, AND THE BISHOPS.` · `I WILL NOT HAND THEM OVER.` · `NOT FOR A MOUNTAIN OF GOLD.`

segments.voice: The practice: protect a guest. Settle into your breath. Then think about who is a guest in your life right now: someone new at work, a family that just moved onto your street, a friend of a friend at the table, a relative staying with you. Who might they need protecting from? Loneliness, a joke at their expense, a rule they don't know yet. Picture one of them. Find one way, this week, that you'll stand between them and whatever makes them feel unwelcome. Hold that picture while you sit. The bell holds the time.
The Negus weeps. The Christian king of Abyssinia hears surah Maryam, weeps, and refuses to hand the Muslims over, not for a mountain of gold. Today's word.
Your line: the king wept. Today, when someone new is in a room with you, be the one who makes sure they're not left alone in it. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: The boycott
745.hook: Quraysh boycott the Prophet's clan, who live three years in a valley near starvation
745.howItsDone: Muslims retell the boycott in sirah lessons as the time the Prophet's clan was confined to the valley of Abu Talib, and point to the clan's loyalty, believers and unbelievers together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Negus weeps, and the emigrants are safe across the sea. Your line was: the king wept. Who was the guest you looked out for? Day seven hundred forty-five.

No sword, this time. No rock on anyone's chest. Just a sheet of writing. Back in Mecca, Ibn Ishaq says, the leaders of Quraysh saw the Muslims safe in Abyssinia, saw Hamzah and Umar on the Prophet's side, and saw the message spreading among the clans. So they tried something slower. They drew up a document, agreed to it together, and hung it inside the Ka'ba, to make it binding. It was aimed at one family. Today: the boycott.
screen: `NO SWORD, JUST A DOCUMENT.` → `HUNG INSIDE THE KA'BA.` → `AIMED AT ONE FAMILY.`

segments.voice: The terms, as Ibn Ishaq gives them, were simple. No one would marry into the clans of Hashim and al-Muttalib, or give them anyone in marriage. No one would sell to them, or buy from them. Cut off the family, and the man at its center would be handed over or starve with them. The clan didn't hand him over. Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib went with Abu Talib into his valley on the edge of Mecca, the shi'b, and Ibn Ishaq says they went together, believers and unbelievers alike. Abu Lahab, Ibn Ishaq says, left his clan and sided with Quraysh. So the boycott shut in people who did not share the Prophet's faith, only his blood. And they went hungry. Ibn Ishaq says they were worn down, and that almost nothing reached them except what was smuggled in. He tells of Hakim ibn Hizam with a servant carrying wheat for his aunt Khadijah, until Abu Jahl caught him and tried to stop it, and another Meccan stepped in and let the food pass. How long did it last? Ibn Ishaq says two or three years; today's line rounds it to three years hungry. A document hung inside the Ka'ba, used to starve a family. The family's answer was to stay together.
screen: `NO MARRIAGE, NO TRADE.` · `INTO THE VALLEY, ALL TOGETHER.` · `BLOOD, NOT ONLY FAITH.` · `WHEAT FOR KHADIJAH.`

segments.voice: The practice: go without one thing, and give it. Sit, and breathe, and think about today. What's one thing you'll eat, drink or buy that you could do without: a coffee, a snack, a delivery, a second helping. Choose it now. Then choose where it goes instead: the money to a food bank, the food to a neighbor, the time to someone who's struggling. Notice the small pull of wanting it anyway. In the valley, that pull lasted for years. If you pray, you can remember the hungry by name. The bell holds the time.
The boycott. Quraysh agree in writing to cut off the Prophet's clan, no marriage and no trade, and the clan holds together in the valley, hungry. Today's word.
Your line: three years hungry. Today, the one thing you went without, give it away before the day is out, and let the small hunger remind you who's hungry for real. Day seven hundred forty-five.

screen: `DAY 745 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TERMITE AND THE TREATY.`

746.title: The termite and the treaty
746.hook: the sirah says the boycott document was eaten by termites except the name of Allah
746.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of the termite and the boycott document in sirah lessons, and some teachers point to it as one of the signs given to the Prophet in Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boycott, and a clan shut in the valley. Your line was: three years hungry. What did you go without, and where did it go? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Somewhere inside the Ka'ba, in the dark, the document still hangs. The one Quraysh signed. The one that has kept a whole clan hungry in the valley. Quraysh have no reason to take it down and read it; they know what it says. And all that time, the sirah says, something small has been at work on it, without anyone noticing. Not a person. Not an army. An insect. Today: the termite and the treaty.
screen: `THE DOCUMENT IN THE DARK.` → `NOBODY LOOKS AT IT.` → `SOMETHING SMALL AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq tells it like this. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told his uncle Abu Talib that God had sent the termite against the document, and that it had eaten every word of injustice and broken ties in it, leaving only the place where the name of God was written. Abu Talib asked him: did your Lord tell you this? Yes, he said. So Abu Talib walked out of the valley to the gathering of Quraysh, and made them an offer. My nephew says this. Go and look. If he's lying, I'll hand him over to you. If he's telling the truth, then end this boycott. They went, took down the document, and found it as he had said. Notice what was left. The document opened, as Quraysh's writings of the time did, with the words bismika Allahumma: in your name, O God. Those words were all that remained. The cruelty had been eaten. The name stood. In fairness, the reports differ on the details, and some versions say the opposite: that the name of God was what the termite took, and the rest was left. The sirah also tells of Meccans who were already working to end the boycott, which is tomorrow's story. But in Ibn Ishaq's telling the picture is clear. Words written to starve a family turned out to be fragile. The name of God, written at the top almost as a formality, outlasted them.
screen: `THE TERMITE WAS SENT.` · `GO AND LOOK, SAID ABU TALIB.` · `IN YOUR NAME, O GOD.` · `THE CRUELTY WAS EATEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: look for what survives. Sit, and breathe. Think back over a hard stretch in your life: a bad year, a loss, a time when something unfair had you boxed in. Much of it has faded, or been eaten away. Now look for what's still standing from that time. A friendship that held. A habit of prayer or kindness that started then. A sentence someone said that you still carry. Let the rest fall away for a minute, and look at only that. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The termite and the treaty. The sirah says termites ate the boycott document, all but the words: in your name, O God. Today's word.
screen: `THE TERMITE AND THE TREATY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: only the name remained. Today, when something unfair feels permanent, remember how fragile that document turned out to be, and look for what's still standing. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: The boycott ends
747.hook: some Meccans of conscience tear up the boycott, starting with one man who could no longer eat in peace
747.howItsDone: Muslims learn the end of the boycott as part of the Meccan sirah, and the names of the Meccans who worked to end it are kept in Ibn Ishaq's account and retold in sirah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the termite and the treaty. Your line was: only the name remained. What did you notice that outlasted everything around it? Day seven hundred forty-seven.

A camel is being led through the dark toward the valley where the Prophet's clan is shut in. It is loaded with food. At the mouth of the valley, Ibn Ishaq tells us, the man leading it takes off its halter, strikes it on the flank, and lets it walk in alone, so nobody can say he broke the agreement. His name is Hisham ibn Amr. He is not one of the Prophet's followers. He is a Meccan with relatives inside, and the agreement sits badly with him. Today: the boycott ends, and it ends because a few people like him stop keeping quiet.
screen: `A CAMEL IN THE DARK.` → `FOOD FOR THE VALLEY.` → `A MAN WITH KIN INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq carries it on from there. Hisham goes to a man named Zuhayr, whose mother came from the Prophet's own clan, and asks him a plain question: how can you eat, and dress, and marry, while your mother's family can't buy or sell? Zuhayr answers honestly. What can I do? I'm one man. If I had one more with me, I'd act. So Hisham says: you have one. Me. Zuhayr says, find us another. And Hisham does. He goes to al-Mut'im ibn Adi, then to Abu al-Bakhtari, then to Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, and each time he asks the same question and gets the same answer: not alone. They meet at night above Mecca and agree on a plan. In the morning Zuhayr walks around the Ka'ba and then turns to the crowd and says, in effect: people of Mecca, are we going to eat and wear clothes while this clan perishes? I won't sit down until this unjust, severing document is torn up. Abu Jahl shouts that it will never be torn. And then, one after another, as they planned, the others stand up and say: tear it. Al-Mut'im goes to take the document down, and finds what we heard yesterday: the insects have eaten it, all but the words, in Your name, O Allah. Notice what did the work here. Not an army. Not a miracle alone. A man with food, a question asked out loud, and a promise not to stand by himself. The sirah doesn't present these men as believers in the Prophet's message. It presents them as people who decided a rule was wrong and said so, together. The sirah keeps all five of their names.
screen: `HISHAM ASKS: HOW CAN YOU EAT?` · `ZUHAYR: I'M ONE MAN.` · `ONE BY ONE, THEY JOIN.` · `AT THE KA'BA: TEAR IT UP.` · then, large: `NOT ALONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: speak up against an unfair rule. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one rule, or one habit of a group you're in, that lands hard on someone who can't easily push back. A workplace policy. A family pattern. A rule at school. Don't fix it yet. Just see it clearly. Then do what Hisham did: name one person who might stand up with you. Picture asking them. And then shape one sentence you could say out loud, short and fair, the way Zuhayr did at the Ka'ba. Some who pray ask Allah here for the courage to say it. The bell holds the time.
The boycott ends. In Ibn Ishaq's telling, a handful of Meccans agree one by one, stand up at the Ka'ba, and the document comes down. Today's word.
Your line: conscience ended it. Today, say your one fair sentence to one person, or find the one person who'll stand with you when you do. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

748.title: Khadijah dies
748.hook: Khadijah dies, and in Bukhari's reports he never stops speaking of her
748.howItsDone: Muslims honor Khadijah as a Mother of the Believers; her life and the Prophet's love for her are retold in sirah study, and Muslims pray for mercy on those who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boycott ends. Your line was: conscience ended it. Did you say your one fair sentence, or find someone to stand with you? Day seven hundred forty-eight.

In Medina, years after the events we're following, a sheep has been slaughtered in the Prophet's household. He cuts it into portions, and sends some out, not to his companions, but to a few women around the city. Aisha, his wife, watches this happen again and again. Who are they? They are the friends of a woman she never met. The boycott is over, and a new part of the story opens, the part of sorrow. It opens with a loss that he carried for the rest of his life. Today: Khadijah dies.
screen: `A SHEEP, CUT INTO PORTIONS.` → `SENT TO OLD FRIENDS.` → `WHOSE FRIENDS?`

segments.voice: Khadijah was the one he ran home to when the revelation began, the one who wrapped him up and said that God would never disgrace him. She was his wife and his shelter, and, as the sirah tells it, she stood beside him through the hungry years in the valley. Then, after the boycott, she dies. The sources are short about the death itself. What they keep, at length, is what came after. Aisha, in Sahih al-Bukhari, is frank about it. She says she was never jealous of any woman the way she was of Khadijah, though she had never seen her, because the Prophet mentioned her so often. And that detail of the sheep, the portions sent to Khadijah's friends, comes from the same report. Another report in Bukhari is even smaller and even more telling. Khadijah's sister, Hala, comes to the door one day and asks permission to come in. Something in the way she asks, her voice, her manner, is like Khadijah's. And he is shaken by it, and calls out, O Allah, Hala. Years after her death, a voice at the door could still do that. In Sahih Muslim he puts it in his own words: he was given her love. Not that he chose it, or earned it. It was given. And Bukhari also reports that Jibril told him to give Khadijah good news of a house in Paradise, a place with no noise in it and no tiredness. Hold those together. The grief is real. The love is called a gift. And the memory shows up in ordinary things: meat for her friends, a sister's knock.
screen: `THE ONE HE RAN HOME TO.` · `AISHA: NEVER SO JEALOUS.` · `A SISTER'S VOICE AT THE DOOR.` · `HER LOVE WAS GIVEN TO HIM.` · then, large: `MEAT FOR HER FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: speak of someone you've lost. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one person who is gone. It may be a recent loss, or an old one. Let one ordinary detail come back: a voice, a phrase they used, a dish they made, the way they knocked. Stay with it. Then, if you can, say their name out loud, quietly. Say one thing they did that you're glad of. If you pray, you can ask Allah's mercy for them, the way Muslims do for those who have died. If it's too heavy today, just their name is enough. The bell holds the time.
Khadijah dies. And in the hadith, she is still in his speech long after: her friends fed, her sister's voice recognized, her love called a gift. Today's word.
Your line: he never forgot her. Today, tell one person a small story about someone you've lost, or do one small thing for someone they loved. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

749.title: Abu Talib dies
749.hook: the uncle who protected him dies in the same year, and the shield is gone
749.howItsDone: Muslims learn Abu Talib's protection and death as part of the Meccan sirah; Sunni and Shia Muslims understand his faith differently, and Shia Muslims honor him as a believer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khadijah dies. Your line was: he never forgot her. Whose story did you tell, or whose friend did you do something for? Day seven hundred forty-nine.

Dust, thrown from the street onto his head, as he walks home through Mecca. Just dust. A small, humiliating thing. He goes home with it still in his hair, and his daughter gets up to wash it off, and she's crying as she does it. He says to her, don't cry, my daughter, Allah will protect your father. Ibn Ishaq tells this scene, and he adds why it could happen now, when it couldn't before: the man who had kept the street from touching him was gone. Today: Abu Talib dies.
screen: `DUST ON HIS HEAD.` → `HIS DAUGHTER WEEPS.` → `WHY NOW?`

segments.voice: Abu Talib was his uncle, the one who took him in as a boy and, as the sirah tells it, refused again and again to hand him over when the leaders of Quraysh came asking. He led the clan into the valley during the boycott rather than give him up. He was the shield. Then, in the same year as Khadijah, Ibn Ishaq says, he is dying. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene at his bedside. The Prophet comes in and finds two leaders of Quraysh already there, Abu Jahl among them. He says to his uncle: say there is no god but Allah, a word I can plead for you with before Allah. The two men answer at once: will you leave the religion of Abd al-Muttalib? In Bukhari's report his last words hold to the religion of Abd al-Muttalib, his father. The Prophet says he will keep asking forgiveness for him unless he's forbidden. Muslims read this scene in different ways. In the Sunni hadith collections, it stands as the account of his death, and the report itself links it to two verses, one of them in surah twenty-eight, saying that the Prophet does not guide whom he loves; Allah guides whom He wills. Shia Muslims hold that Abu Talib was a believer who kept his faith quiet to keep his protection strong, and they honor him as such. Both remember the same thing about his life: he protected his nephew when it cost him. And then the protection was gone. The dust in the street is how the sirah shows it. That is what a shield is. Often nobody sees it until it isn't there. And this week has been full of shields: a just king across the sea, Meccans of conscience, a wife who held him up. Today, at home in Mecca, the shield of his own clan falls.
screen: `THE UNCLE WHO WOULDN'T HAND HIM OVER.` · `SAY THE WORD, UNCLE.` · `SUNNI AND SHIA READINGS.` · `A SHIELD IS SEEN WHEN IT'S GONE.` · then, large: `THE SHIELD IS GONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a protector while you can. Settle and breathe. Think back over your life for the people who stood between you and something hard. A parent, an older sibling, a teacher who covered for you, a friend who said no, leave them alone. Some of them never told you. Pick one who is still living. Let yourself see what they actually did, and what it might have cost them. Then decide how you'll thank them: a message, a call, a sentence the next time you see them. Muslims often ask Allah to reward such a person; if you pray, you can too. The bell holds the time.
Abu Talib dies. The uncle who protected him through the boycott is gone, and the street can reach him. Today's word.
Your line: the shield is gone. Today, send the thanks you planned to one person who protected you, before another day passes. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
